name: csjh wasm-interpreter (in-place WebAssembly interpreter)
workload: Startup (load, validate and instantiate) of a large module (SpiderMonkey compiled to Wasm) in a tail-call in-place interpreter, versus Wasmtime, as reported in the author's blog post 'A Tale of Three WebAssembly Runtimes'.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: Wasmtime 183.3 ms versus in-place interpreter 35.4 ms on SpiderMonkey startup (numbers as relayed by a search-result summary of the blog post; the post itself was not readable).
tradeoffs: Interpreter only, so peak throughput is expected to be far below Wasmtime's Cranelift JIT; the win is cheap startup because no compilation pass is needed. Small hobby codebase (C++ with instance.cpp, module.cpp, main.cpp), no WASI breadth claimed.
caveats: Snippet only: csjh.blog is blocked by the egress proxy (EGRESS_BLOCKED), so the numbers come from a web-search summary of the post and were not verified. The repo README is a single heading and carries no benchmark code, compiler, flags or CPU model. Startup only; execution throughput was not reported in the snippet. Wasmtime configuration (Cranelift versus Winch, eager versus lazy compile) unknown. Last commit is a merged spec-test fix (trunc_sat).
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Show HN WebAssembly runtime fast interpreter JIT written from scratch faster than wasmtime' surfaced csjh.blog 'A Tale of Three WebAssembly Runtimes'; repo found at github.com/csjh (repositories tab).

name: Mitey JIT (csjh/mitey-jit)
workload: Unrolled-interpreter JIT for WebAssembly on Arm64 macOS (handlers called from generated code, musttail dispatch); blog post compares it with Wasmtime and Node on esbuild compiled to Wasm and on SpiderMonkey startup.
claimed_speedup: Snippet only: described as a JIT that beats Node and even Wasmtime on esbuild; SpiderMonkey startup 52.8 ms for the unrolled JIT versus 183.3 ms for Wasmtime (numbers relayed by a search-result summary of the blog post, not read directly).
compiler_and_flags: Clang only: relies on [[clang::musttail]], __attribute__((noinline)) and __attribute__((preserve_most)); optimization level not stated.
hardware: Arm64 macOS (README: 'Currently only expected to support Arm64 on MacOS'); CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: Arm64 macOS only, Clang only, README says 'Not meant for production use' although it passes the Wasm spec tests. Uses mmap/mprotect for out-of-bounds handling and a guard-page stack. Repo holds two backends (minimal and baseline single-pass).
caveats: Snippet only: the blog post (csjh.blog) is blocked by the egress proxy, the README contains optimization notes but no benchmark numbers, and no benchmark code is in the repo. No LICENSE file is listed in the repository tree, so usability is reference. The 'beats Wasmtime and Node on esbuild' sentence comes from a search-result summary and the workload details (Wasmtime config, Node version, input) are unknown. Performance claim is probably single-machine and may not generalize to x86-64.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Show HN WebAssembly runtime fast interpreter JIT written from scratch faster than wasmtime' (summary mentioned a JIT beating Node and Wasmtime on esbuild) and 'csjh A Tale of Three WebAssembly Runtimes ... unrolled interpreter JIT'; repo found at github.com/csjh.

name: Wizard Research Engine
baseline: interpreter tiers of other WebAssembly engines (unnamed in the README)
workload: Hand-written x86-64 in-place Wasm interpreter (no bytecode rewriting) versus Wizard's own simple interpreter and, per README, versus interpreter tiers in other engines.
claimed_speedup: README: fast x86-64-linux interpreter is 'nearly 40x faster than the simple interpreter, and as fast as interpreter tiers in other engines'. No numbers against a named external engine on the page.
stars_or_usage: 514 stars; subject of the OOPSLA 2022 paper 'A fast in-place interpreter for WebAssembly'
tradeoffs: Written in Virgil, not C++, and the fast interpreter is hand-written x86-64 assembly for Linux only; README says the design favors flexibility and readability for research over ultimate performance. Benefit of in-place interpretation is low memory use and no rewrite step. WASI support is a work in progress.
caveats: Tier D research entry: the README gives no external baseline numbers and the paper (arXiv 2205.01183, ACM, Tufts copy) was not readable because those hosts are blocked, so any comparison with wasm3 or WAMR is unverified here. In-place interpretation is not claimed to beat the fastest rewriting interpreters (wasm3) on raw speed; the paper's claim is parity with a custom internal format plus lower setup time and space, which could not be checked. doc/ holds only benchmark_analysis_ideas.txt, no results. Worth a verifier pass that can reach the paper.
found_via: Blogs / talks: WebSearch 'Wizard engine WebAssembly Titzer Virgil fast in-place interpreter github wizard-engine benchmark' and the 'WebAssembly interpreter tail calls faster than wasm3' query that surfaced the in-place interpreter paper.
